title: Ali in the house
hookLine: young Ali, Abu Talib's son, is raised in the Prophet's home

cards: A hard year comes to Mecca. Ibn Ishaq calls it a severe famine, and says it hit Quraysh badly. One house feels it hard: Abu Talib's.

He's the uncle who took in an orphaned nephew years before and gave him a place at the table. Now Abu Talib has a big family and not enough to feed them. And the nephew, grown now and married to Khadijah, has an idea.

teach.h: A PLAN TO LIGHTEN THE LOAD.
teach.b: Day seven hundred eleven gave this plan in a sentence. Here it is up close, as Ibn Ishaq tells it.

The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ goes to another uncle, al-Abbas: your brother Abu Talib has a large family, and you can see how hard things are. Let's lighten his load. I'll take one of his sons, you take one.
Al-Abbas agrees, and they ask Abu Talib together.
So two boys change houses that year. Al-Abbas takes Ja'far. The Prophet takes Ali, a small boy, into his home with Khadijah, where he joins Zayd, the boy who chose to stay.
A household that keeps making room. Ibn Ishaq says Ali stayed with him from then on, and when revelation came, Ali followed him and believed. Later, the paths read Ali's place in more than one way.

Sunni tradition counts him among the rightly guided caliphs; Shia tradition holds him to be the Imam after the Prophet. But here he is still a child at Khadijah's table. Ali wasn't an orphan; his father was alive.
The man who took him in had been one, though.
And in Sahih al-Bukhari, that man says the one who looks after an orphan will be with him in Paradise like this, holding up two fingers side by side.
The house that raised Ali was run by someone who knew what that care was worth.

how: Muslims who sponsor or care for orphans often recall the Prophet's ﷺ words about the two fingers side by side, and Ali's upbringing in his home is told when Muslims remember Ali.

s: the two-fingers hadith is about raising your own children
it is about the one who looks after an orphan, in Sahih al-Bukhari.
the idea came from the Prophet
he went to al-Abbas and proposed that each take one of Abu Talib's sons.
Sunni and Shia Muslims both honor Ali
Sunni Muslims as a rightly guided caliph, Shia Muslims as the Imam after the Prophet.

games.q: famine, and your uncle, who raised you, has more children than he can feed. what do you do?
o: send him what money you can spare.
ask another uncle to join you, and each take a son.
wait for the year to turn.
games.why: he went to al-Abbas, and they each took a son into their homes. Ali came to the house where the Prophet lived.

practice: Think of a child in your world who isn't yours, a niece, a neighbor's kid, a student, or of an adult who did that for you when you were small. Ask one plain question: what would lighten the load?
A meal, a ride, an hour, a kind word to a tired parent; if you pray, pray for that child by name.

wordCard.voice: Ali. Abu Talib's young son, taken into the Prophet's own home with Khadijah in a hard year, and raised there. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: taking someone into your care and providing for them, the word used for looking after an orphan.

carryVoice: Your line: raised in that house. A home that kept making room. Seven hundred twenty days now.

sources.ref: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (the famine; the Prophet and al-Abbas each take a son of Abu Talib; Ali stays with him and believes)
Sahih al-Bukhari 5304 (the one who looks after an orphan, like these two fingers)
